subject: history
title: Henry VII and the Henrician Reformation
welcome_lead: focus on dynastic consolidation and Henry VIII's Royal Supremacy.
meta_desc: A-Level Tudors 1485-1603 adventure on Henry VII's consolidation and Henry VIII's break with Rome 1534.
final_note: You can explain Tudor state-building and religious revolution in terms.

concepts.def: 22 August 1485 victory of Henry Tudor over Richard III, beginning Tudor rule.
Henry VII's prerogative tribunal (notably under Empson and Dudley) enforcing royal financial rights.
Alliance with Spain securing the Aragon-Tudor match; Catherine of Aragon married Arthur in 1501, then Henry VIII in 1509.
Statute drafted by Cromwell declaring England 'an empire' free from papal jurisdiction; enabled the Boleyn marriage.
Established by the Act of Supremacy 1534 making Henry VIII Supreme Head of the Church of England.
Major northern rising led by Robert Aske protesting the dissolution; suppressed by 1537 with the execution of about 216 rebels.

walkthroughs.body_html: Henry dated his reign from 21 August 1485, the day before Bosworth, to retrospectively brand opponents traitors. The 1486 marriage to Elizabeth of York united Lancaster and York. Acts of Resumption recovered Crown lands; the Court of Star Chamber (1487 Act) and the Council Learned tightened control. The Treaty of Etaples (1492) extracted French pensions; the Treaty of Medina del Campo (1489) anchored the Spanish alliance.

Catherine of Aragon failed to produce a male heir. Henry's reading of Leviticus 20:21 framed his marriage as cursed. Wolsey's failure at Blackfriars (1529) ended his career. Anne Boleyn's faction promoted reform; Thomas Cromwell entered royal service and used Parliament (the 'Reformation Parliament', 1529-36).

The Act in Restraint of Appeals (1533) preceded Cranmer's annulment. The Act of Supremacy (November 1534), Treason Act (1534) and Act of Succession crystallised the new order. Dissolution proceeded in two waves: lesser houses (1536) and greater (1539). The Pilgrimage of Grace (October-December 1536) was the largest Tudor rebellion. The 1539 Act of Six Articles re-asserted Catholic doctrine, balancing Cromwell's reforms.
